records.sourceFile: The influence of limb dominance on performance-based outcomes after ACL reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Hodges J, Bruce Leicht AS, Thompson XD, Werner BC, Diduch DR, Brockmeier SF, et al. The Influence of Limb Dominance on Performance-Based Outcomes After ACL Reconstruction. Sports Health. 2025.
paper.abstract: In 279 patients tested about 7.7 months after ACL reconstruction, limb dominance was associated with the pass status of isometric knee extension LSI, with dominant-limb surgery achieving more symmetric knee extension torque and higher pass rates. No other strength, balance or hop LSI pass status was associated with limb dominance. Raw strength and balance measures did not differ, and small differences were found in the 6-meter hop, COP distance and contralateral triple hop.
paper.tldr: After ACL reconstruction, surgery on the dominant leg went with more symmetric isometric knee extension strength, but limb dominance did not change most other strength, balance or hop results. Consider limb dominance when reading knee extension LSI, but do not treat it as a reason to change standard criteria.
paper.methods: Observational cross-sectional study at a university laboratory of patients 5.5 to 12 months after primary, unilateral ACL reconstruction. Patients completed isokinetic and isometric knee strength, COP balance, and single-leg hop, triple hop and 6-meter hop tests, and LSI was classified as pass at 90% or more. Limb dominance was the preferred kicking leg, and comparisons used chi-square and independent t tests.
paper.findings: Isometric knee extension LSI pass status was associated with limb dominance (chi-square 10.09, P=0.001), with 25 of 134 dominant-limb cases and 9 of 145 nondominant-limb cases passing. Isometric knee extension LSI was higher for dominant-limb surgery (73.71 vs 66.50%, P<0.001, d=0.42). COP distance LSI (P=0.03, d=0.40, more symmetric with nondominant-limb surgery) and 6-meter hop LSI (P=0.02, d=0.25) also differed, and contralateral triple-hop distance was greater in the nondominant-limb group (P=0.03, d=0.23).
paper.limitations: The sample was mostly older adolescents and young adults and was not described by athletic status. Some tests were incomplete, balance data were added later, rehabilitation compliance was not controlled, and limb dominance was defined by kicking leg, which the authors note is subjective. The design cannot show cause, and most significant differences had small effect sizes with LSI values near 100%.
paper.practicalImplications: When a return-to-activity decision relies on knee extension LSI, clinicians may consider whether the surgery was on the dominant leg, since more dominant-limb cases passed the 90% cut-off for isometric extension. The authors advise caution because the dominance definition is subjective and most other measures were unaffected, so limb dominance should complement standard LSI criteria rather than replace them.
paper.athleteDev: Limb dominance changed isometric knee extension symmetry in these patients after ACL reconstruction, so knee extension strength targets may be read with the dominance side in mind. The sample was not described as athletes, and the study did not test training methods, so it does not show which program corrects these differences.
paper.rtp: The study can inform how clinicians read LSI at return-to-activity testing, but it cannot show that limb dominance changes reinjury risk or the timing of clearance. The authors call for future work on reinjury and on tailored rehabilitation for dominance-specific asymmetries.

records.sourceFile: The return to sport clearance continuum is a novel approach toward return to sport and performance for the professional athlete.pdf

paper.citation: Draovitch P, Patel S, Marrone W, Grundstein MJ, Grant R, Virgile A, et al. The return-to-sport clearance continuum is a novel approach toward return to sport and performance for the professional athlete. Arthroscopy, Sports Medicine, and Rehabilitation. 2022;4(1):e93-e101.
paper.abstract: The authors argue that return to sport for professional athletes should be an evolving continuum of criterion-based checks, not a single decision at one point in time. The article presents the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum with five phases and describes progressive, regular qualitative and quantitative testing to help athletes return at their maximal performance level. The level of evidence is V, expert opinion.
paper.tldr: The authors propose the Return to Sport Clearance Continuum, which treats return to sport as a series of criterion-based checkpoints with regular testing and load monitoring. It is a proposed framework that has not been tested against outcomes.
paper.methods: Expert-opinion clinical review. The authors describe a five-phase continuum and summarise common return-to-sport tests (strength and limb symmetry, hop, balance, qualitative movement and force-plate measures) for lower-extremity injuries. No literature search method is described.
paper.findings: The authors present return to sport as criterion-based and continuous rather than time-based. They cite studies linking objective criteria or longer delays before return with lower reinjury rates, and note that limb symmetry indices can overestimate knee function. The continuum itself was not tested in data.
paper.limitations: The framework is expert opinion (Level V) with no sample, no outcome data and no validity or reliability testing of the continuum. The authors note that the extent of movement analysis will vary with institutional resources such as 3D motion analysis and force plates. The evidence cited is drawn mainly from lower-extremity injury studies, especially ACL reconstruction.
paper.practicalImplications: Use a set of checkpoints across the recovery process, with both quantitative and qualitative tests, instead of relying on a single clearance test or on time since injury. Share the current phase and its criteria across the physician, therapist, strength coach and athlete so that expectations match.
paper.athleteDev: After return, the paper recommends a preseason plan that manages loads, repetitions and days off, with load monitoring continuing through the season. It also notes that success in the first year after injury does not guarantee success later, and that joint health after ACL reconstruction may take up to 2 years to return to baseline.
paper.rtp: The framework supports progressing athletes through phases on criteria rather than time alone, with strength, hop, balance and movement testing at each stage. It does not give validated pass thresholds or a clearance rule, so it cannot make a return-to-play decision on its own.

records.sourceFile: The role of strength-related factors on psychological readiness for return to sport following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Lee OT, Williams MA, Shaw CD, Delextrat A. The Role of Strength-Related Factors on Psychological Readiness for Return to Sport Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Reconstruction. Healthcare. 2023;11:2787.
paper.abstract: Twelve athletes more than nine months after ACL reconstruction completed the ACL-RSI questionnaire and isokinetic testing of the hamstrings and quadriceps at 60 and 180 deg/s. Athletes were split into cases and controls by ACL-RSI score. RTD and time since surgery were determinants of psychological readiness, and cases showed lower quadriceps torque near full knee extension and lower RTD than controls, with no peak torque difference.
paper.tldr: In 12 athletes after ACL reconstruction, lower quadriceps rate of torque development and lower torque near full knee extension went with lower psychological readiness for return to sport. The study is small and cross-sectional, so it suggests targets for rehabilitation rather than proven causes.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional study. Participants completed the ACL-RSI questionnaire, then isokinetic testing (Biodex System 4) of the operated and non-operated legs at 60 and 180 deg/s. Cases were ACL-RSI below 81.4% (n = 7) and controls above it (n = 5). Stepwise linear regression was run on the whole sample, and a repeated-measures mixed ANOVA compared groups across velocities.
paper.findings: Quadriceps RTD100 at 60 deg/s, time since surgery and hamstring RTD50 at 60 deg/s were significant predictors of ACL-RSI score (r2 = 0.915). Cases had lower quadriceps torque at 40 and 30 degrees from full extension (Qcon40 and Qcon30) than controls, and lower quadriceps RTD100 (95% CI 763 to 1003 vs 979 to 1315 N.m.s-1 for cases vs controls). Peak torque did not differ between groups.
paper.limitations: Only 12 participants, so the group comparisons and the regression are unstable. Rehabilitation type, volume and sport participation were not recorded. The text gives 81.4% as the group threshold but describes controls as scoring above 81.5, a minor inconsistency. The 0-10 degree range was dropped for lack of data.
paper.practicalImplications: Rehabilitation staff may wish to measure RTD and torque near full knee extension alongside peak strength when assessing readiness after ACL reconstruction. The study does not show that training these qualities changes ACL-RSI scores.
paper.athleteDev: For athletes after ACL reconstruction, the study suggests including power and rate-of-force work and strength near full extension in training. These are hypotheses from a small cross-sectional sample, not tested training effects.
paper.rtp: The study can inform return-to-sport planning by highlighting RTD and near-extension quadriceps strength as points to assess in athletes with low psychological readiness. It cannot establish readiness thresholds or clearance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Therapeutic exercises and modalities in athletes with acute hamstring injuries - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Jankaew A, Chen JC, Chamnongkich S, Lin CF. Therapeutic Exercises and Modalities in Athletes With Acute Hamstring Injuries: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Health. 2022.
paper.abstract: In nine randomised trials of 396 athletes with acute hamstring injuries, a loading program during extensive lengthening shortened time to return to play compared with a conventional program. Strengthening with trunk stabilisation and agility reduced reinjury at 12 months but did not significantly shorten time to return to play, and the evidence on stretching and physical modalities was too limited to pool.
paper.tldr: For athletes with acute hamstring injuries, eccentric loading during lengthening was linked with a faster return to play, and strengthening with trunk and agility work was linked with fewer reinjuries at 12 months. The evidence rests on few small trials, mostly in male athletes.
paper.methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis following PRISMA and the Cochrane Handbook, with five databases searched from inception to July 2021 and registration on PROSPERO. Included studies were RCTs of exercise-based or physical-modality treatment in athletes with acute hamstring injuries. Quality was rated with the PEDro scale, and outcomes (time to return to play, pain and reinjury rate) were pooled with fixed or random effects models in RevMan.
paper.findings: Nine RCTs were included from 24 full texts assessed. Loading during lengthening versus conventional exercise: time to return to play was 28.29 days shorter (mean difference -28.29, 95% CI -41.60 to -14.99, P < 0.0001), and reinjury did not differ (risk difference -0.05, P = 0.17). Strengthening with trunk stabilisation and agility versus other programs: time to return to play did not differ (mean difference -3.78 days, 95% CI -9.04 to 1.48, P = 0.16), reinjury at 6 months did not differ (risk difference -0.00, P = 0.97), and at 12 months reinjury was lower (risk difference -0.41, 95% CI -0.70 to -0.11, P < 0.007, two studies). Stretching programs and physical modalities could not be pooled.
paper.limitations: Nine small RCTs with 396 participants (317 men, 79 women). The paper describes them as 93.69% male, which does not match its own counts (317 of 396 is about 80%). Quality scores ranged from 3 to 9 with little blinding or concealed allocation, and the two loading trials pooled for return to play scored 4 and 5 with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 58%). Acute injury was defined differently across trials (2 to 10 days), most trials compared active programs rather than a true control, the 12-month reinjury estimate comes from two studies, and the effect of physical modalities cannot be separated from exercise.
paper.practicalImplications: In the early phase of an acute hamstring injury, a loading program during extensive lengthening can be considered where a faster return to play is the priority, and trunk stabilisation with agility work can be considered where reducing reinjury is the priority. The review could not draw conclusions on stretching programs or physical modalities alone because those trials could not be pooled.
paper.athleteDev: The study concerns rehabilitation of acute injuries and measures no performance outcomes. Its exercise content, such as eccentric loading during lengthening and trunk and agility work, may inform progressive reconditioning, but the review does not test performance.
paper.rtp: The loading program is linked with a shorter time to return to play (pooled 28.29 days faster versus the conventional program), so it is the main option supported by this review for return-to-sport planning. Strengthening with trunk and agility work is supported for reducing 12-month reinjury, not for speeding return. The evidence does not cover return-to-sport criteria or RTP testing.
